title: RTO and RPO for Azure applications
description: Quantify recovery objectives for Azure workloads. Map RTO and RPO to Azure services, understand trade-offs between cost and speed, and choose the right replication and backup tier for your application.

data.text: RTO and RPO are the two numbers that determine every disaster recovery decision. RTO is how quickly you must restore service after an outage. RPO is how much data you can afford to lose. Together, they shape your choice of Azure services, replication technology, and backup frequency.

Recovery Time Objective (RTO) is measured in minutes or hours. It starts when the outage begins and ends when the service is fully operational again. Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is measured in data. If your RPO is five minutes, you must have a copy of data from no older than five minutes before the outage.

terms.definition: Recovery Time Objective: the maximum acceptable downtime after an incident.
Recovery Point Objective: the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time.
Recovery Level Objective: the granularity of recovery, such as item-level or database-level.

rows: Multi-write or single-write with multiple regions

data.text: Lower RTO and RPO cost more money. Active geo-replication for SQL Database replicates data synchronously to a secondary region, but you pay for the secondary server. Azure Backup is cheap but slow. There is no universal 'best' setting; the right choice depends on business impact. A customer-facing checkout service may justify a 30-second RTO, while an internal reporting dashboard may tolerate a 4-hour RTO.

data.title: Test your recovery
data.text: An RTO that exists only on paper is useless. Run failover drills regularly and measure the actual time to restore service. Azure Site Recovery and auto-failover groups make testing possible without risking data.

data.title: Setting recovery objectives
items: Classify applications by business impact: critical, important, or standard.
Assign RTO and RPO targets for each class.
Map each target to Azure service tiers and replication technologies.
Validate recovery time with a non-production failover test.
Review and adjust targets annually or after major architecture changes.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: RTO measures downtime; RPO measures data loss.
Faster recovery costs more—balance targets against business value.
Azure services offer a spectrum from backup to active geo-replication.
Untested recovery plans are not plans; they are assumptions.
data.takeaway: Choose your Azure replication tier by starting with business RTO and RPO, then work backward to service configuration.
